policy.safety_scope: Conceptual study questions only. Exact aircraft procedures, limitations, and operational decisions require current approved aircraft and operator documentation.

questions.question: What does NEO mean in A321neo, and what does the name identify?

expected_key_facts.fact: NEO means New Engine Option.
A321neo is an A320 Family aircraft variant.

acceptable_concepts: It is a narrow-body A320 Family variant with new-engine options.
NEO describes the engine-option generation, not a separate aircraft family.
important_incorrect_concepts: NEO means new electric operation.
NEO identifies a wide-body aircraft.

questions.question: What broad kind of aircraft is the Airbus A321neo?

expected_key_facts.fact: The A321neo is a narrow-body commercial jet.
It has two engines.

acceptable_concepts: A twin-engine, single-aisle commercial transport.
A member of the A320neo family.
important_incorrect_concepts: It is a four-engine wide-body.
It is a single-engine aircraft.

questions.question: Why should a pilot separate the selected state, active mode, and actual aircraft response?

expected_key_facts.fact: The selected state is what the crew requests or enters.
The active mode is what the aircraft is currently using.
The aircraft response is what the aircraft actually does.
Separating them helps diagnose selection, mode, data, or system problems.

acceptable_concepts: Compare the request, annunciated mode, and measured result.
Use the distinction to avoid treating a selector position as proof of aircraft behavior.
important_incorrect_concepts: The selected target always guarantees the aircraft response.
The selector alone is the authoritative indication of the active mode.
question_requirements: explain why the three states differ

questions.question: Why does weight and balance matter for A321neo performance?

expected_key_facts.fact: Weight affects acceleration, climb, stopping, and available performance margins.
Center of gravity affects stability, control, and performance.
Operational values must come from approved aircraft-specific performance data.

acceptable_concepts: Mass changes energy and required performance; mass distribution changes trim and handling.
Use current approved calculations rather than a generic rule.
important_incorrect_concepts: A generic rule can replace approved performance calculation.
CG has no effect if total weight is unchanged.

questions.question: How does an autopilot work conceptually?

expected_key_facts.fact: The autopilot compares aircraft state with active guidance targets.
It uses control laws and feedback to command the aircraft.
The crew must monitor the mode and aircraft response.

acceptable_concepts: It is a closed-loop guidance function using targets, sensed state, computation, and control commands.
The explanation includes mode awareness and monitoring.
important_incorrect_concepts: The autopilot removes the need for monitoring.
It independently understands pilot intent without selected or managed targets.

questions.question: How does the FMGS work at a conceptual level?

expected_key_facts.fact: The FMGS combines route, navigation, performance, aircraft-state, and database information.
It produces predictions and lateral or vertical guidance.
The exact result depends on aircraft standard, software, database, and inputs.

acceptable_concepts: It integrates entered intent with navigation and aircraft data to compute predictions and guidance.
Outputs remain dependent on configuration and data quality.
important_incorrect_concepts: The FMGS guarantees the aircraft will follow every plan.
The database alone determines all guidance without aircraft-state inputs.

questions.question: What is the conceptual difference between managed and selected guidance?

expected_key_facts.fact: Managed guidance uses the flight-management profile or targets.
Selected guidance uses a crew-selected FCU target or mode.
The FMA must be checked to confirm the active and armed modes.

acceptable_concepts: Managed guidance follows computed or programmed intent; selected guidance follows a crew-selected target or mode.
The FMA shows what is active or armed.
important_incorrect_concepts: Managed is always safer than selected.
The FCU selection alone proves the mode is active.

questions.question: How should an A320 and A321neo comparison be framed without overgeneralizing?

expected_key_facts.fact: They share A320 Family design and operating concepts.
Size, weight, engines, configuration, and performance can differ.
Exact procedures and limits must be checked for the aircraft standard and operator.

acceptable_concepts: Start with commonality, then name variant-specific differences.
Use aircraft- and operator-specific documentation for operational claims.
important_incorrect_concepts: All A320 Family procedures and limits are identical.
The A321neo is merely an A320 with no performance differences.

questions.question: If the aircraft does not capture the expected altitude, what should be checked first in a simulator study?

expected_key_facts.fact: Check the selected altitude and relevant FCU input.
Check the FMA for active or armed vertical modes.
Check constraints, aircraft energy or state, and data before blaming the system.

acceptable_concepts: Record the selection, annunciation, constraints, and actual trend before diagnosing failure.
Change one simulator assumption at a time.
important_incorrect_concepts: The autopilot is definitely failed.
A selected altitude alone proves that capture should occur.
question_requirements: avoid declaring a system failure immediately

questions.question: What should be done when the FMA does not match what the crew expected?

expected_key_facts.fact: Treat the FMA as the indication of active or armed modes, not the selector alone.
Recheck the selection, engagement conditions, constraints, and aircraft state.
Use the applicable approved procedure for an operational event.

acceptable_concepts: Compare intended mode with annunciated mode and investigate inputs and conditions.
Escalate to the applicable procedure when the situation is operational.
important_incorrect_concepts: Ignore the FMA if the selector looks correct.
The unexpected annunciation is automatically a hardware failure.

questions.question: What information does the FMA provide and why is it important?

expected_key_facts.fact: The FMA shows relevant active and armed guidance or autothrust modes.
It lets the crew compare the aircraft mode with the intended selection.
It is part of monitoring automation and does not replace procedural guidance.

acceptable_concepts: The FMA is a mode-awareness and automation-monitoring source.
It helps detect divergence between intent and active behavior.
important_incorrect_concepts: The FMA is only a decorative status display.
It replaces all other aircraft indications and procedures.

questions.question: How are the MCDU and FMGS related at a conceptual level?

expected_key_facts.fact: The MCDU is a crew interface used to enter and review information for the FMGS.
The FMGS uses route, performance, navigation, and aircraft-state information.
Entries and resulting guidance must be cross-checked against the current aircraft and database.

acceptable_concepts: The MCDU is an interface; the FMGS is the broader management and guidance function.
Crew entries become inputs that must be checked against indications and source data.
important_incorrect_concepts: The MCDU directly controls every actuator.
A displayed prediction is automatically a guaranteed aircraft result.

questions.question: Why must route and performance entries in the MCDU be checked rather than blindly accepted?

expected_key_facts.fact: Incorrect entries or assumptions can produce incorrect predictions or guidance.
Database status, aircraft configuration, and required inputs affect the result.
The crew should cross-check entries and indications with approved procedures and sources.

acceptable_concepts: Successful data entry is not the same as validated operational intent.
Independent checks should include data, configuration, and resulting indications.
important_incorrect_concepts: A successful entry proves the plan is operationally correct.
The database removes the need for crew verification.

questions.question: What is the relationship between an FCU selection and the FMA indication?

expected_key_facts.fact: The FCU is used for relevant crew-selected targets or mode selections.
The FMA indicates which modes are active or armed.
A selection alone does not prove that the expected mode is active.

acceptable_concepts: The FCU expresses intent or a selected target; the FMA confirms mode status.
The two should be read together with aircraft response.
important_incorrect_concepts: The FCU display always shows the active mode.
Turning a selector guarantees engagement.
question_requirements: explain why they must be compared

questions.question: Why do automation priorities and monitoring tasks change across flight phases?

expected_key_facts.fact: Takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, approach, and landing have different energy and guidance priorities.
Targets, constraints, configuration, and active modes can change with the phase.
The crew must monitor the applicable phase-specific procedure and aircraft response.

acceptable_concepts: The same automation label can have different implications as energy, configuration, and constraints change.
Phase awareness is part of monitoring.
important_incorrect_concepts: One automation mode is universally correct for every phase.
A mode change removes the need to monitor the aircraft.

questions.question: Which inputs commonly affect takeoff or landing performance, and how should the result be used?

expected_key_facts.fact: Weight, temperature, pressure or altitude, wind, runway characteristics, slope, obstacles, and configuration can affect performance.
The result should come from approved aircraft-specific performance data.
Generic model output should not be used as an operational clearance or limitation.

acceptable_concepts: Name several environmental, aircraft, runway, and loading inputs.
State that approved data determines the operational result.
important_incorrect_concepts: A fixed generic distance is valid for every runway and weight.
A simulator estimate can replace approved performance data.
question_requirements: state how to use the result safely

questions.question: In a simulator, an altitude capture looks unexpected. How should the scenario be analyzed?

expected_key_facts.fact: Record the selected target, active or armed FMA modes, and actual aircraft response.
Check aircraft state, constraints, inputs, and simulator or model configuration.
Change one assumption or variable at a time and compare expected with observed behavior.

acceptable_concepts: Use a controlled observation-and-comparison method.
Keep simulator fidelity and real-aircraft authority as separate questions.
important_incorrect_concepts: Simulator behavior alone proves the real aircraft has the same behavior.
A single surprising result identifies the failed component.

questions.question: A simulator route behaves differently after a flight-plan edit. What should the trainee investigate?

expected_key_facts.fact: Verify the edited route, constraints, discontinuities, and active guidance.
Check navigation database status and simulator aircraft or software version.
Do not assume the observed result is a real-aircraft procedure or limitation without authoritative confirmation.

acceptable_concepts: Reconstruct the edit and compare the expected route computation with the displayed active result.
Check data and model version.
important_incorrect_concepts: The simulator is an authoritative replacement for current aircraft documentation.
Any route accepted by the interface is automatically valid.
question_requirements: separate simulator behavior from operational authority

questions.question: What is the main structural relationship between the A320neo and A321neo?

expected_key_facts.fact: Both are members of the A320neo family.
The A321neo is the larger, longer-fuselage member of the pair.

acceptable_concepts: They share a family architecture but are not identical aircraft.
The A321neo has a longer fuselage and different mass or performance characteristics.
important_incorrect_concepts: The A321neo is a wide-body derivative.
The two variants have identical weights and performance.

questions.question: What is the purpose of fly-by-wire in the A320 family?

expected_key_facts.fact: Pilot or automatic inputs are processed by flight-control computers.
The computers command control surfaces or actuators through the applicable control laws.

acceptable_concepts: It is a digital flight-control architecture between inputs, computers, and actuators.
The control-law layer shapes how inputs become aircraft response.
important_incorrect_concepts: The sidestick is mechanically connected directly to every surface.
Fly-by-wire means the computers can ignore all pilot inputs.
question_requirements: describe the computer and actuator roles

questions.question: What broad role does the ECAM have on an A320-family flight deck?

expected_key_facts.fact: ECAM presents engine and system information to the crew.
It supports monitoring and awareness but does not replace the applicable procedure or source.

acceptable_concepts: It organizes system and engine indications for flight-deck monitoring.
Its indications must be interpreted in context.
important_incorrect_concepts: ECAM is a flight-management computer that generates all guidance.
An ECAM page alone replaces a checklist or approved procedure.

questions.question: What is the conceptual purpose of an aircraft trim system?

expected_key_facts.fact: Trim changes the balance of aerodynamic or control forces for a flight condition.
Trim is distinct from commanding the primary maneuver itself.

acceptable_concepts: Trim helps reduce sustained control force or establish an appropriate balance.
The exact implementation depends on aircraft design and mode.
important_incorrect_concepts: Trim is a substitute for controlling airspeed or attitude.
Trim guarantees a fixed flight path regardless of energy or configuration.

questions.question: What does an air data system contribute to flight-deck awareness?

expected_key_facts.fact: It provides processed pressure-derived information such as airspeed, altitude, and vertical trend.
The information supports displays, guidance, and performance computations.

acceptable_concepts: Air-data inputs describe the aircraft's relationship to surrounding air and pressure.
Indications must be cross-checked if data quality is in doubt.
important_incorrect_concepts: Air data directly measures ground track.
One air-data value is always sufficient to establish aircraft state.

questions.question: What is the broad difference between an aircraft system indication and a control command?

expected_key_facts.fact: An indication reports a state, value, or mode.
A command requests or influences a target or action.

acceptable_concepts: A displayed value may describe what exists; a control selection expresses intent.
The observed aircraft response is a separate layer.
important_incorrect_concepts: Every displayed value is a command.
A command proves the aircraft achieved the requested result.

questions.question: What is the basic purpose of an aircraft navigation database?

expected_key_facts.fact: It stores coded navigation and procedure information used by flight-management functions.
Its currency, applicability, and aircraft compatibility matter to the result.

acceptable_concepts: It provides structured data rather than being a live authorization.
The crew must verify the relevant data and source.
important_incorrect_concepts: The database itself is an air traffic clearance.
A database entry is valid for every aircraft and date.

questions.question: Why is a sidestick input not best understood as a direct command to one control surface?

expected_key_facts.fact: The input is processed by the fly-by-wire flight-control architecture.
The resulting surface commands depend on control laws, aircraft state, and configuration.

acceptable_concepts: The sidestick expresses pilot input to a computer-mediated control system.
Aircraft response depends on the current law and state.
important_incorrect_concepts: Moving left always moves one aileron by a fixed amount.
The sidestick is a mechanical yoke connected directly to the surfaces.

questions.question: Why can two aircraft with the same selected speed show different immediate behavior?

expected_key_facts.fact: Mode, energy state, configuration, thrust or drag, and flight phase affect the response.
A selected target is an instruction or target, not a guarantee of instantaneous achievement.

acceptable_concepts: The same target can be approached through different current states and control modes.
Compare target, active mode, trend, and actual value.
important_incorrect_concepts: The selected value forces identical acceleration in every condition.
Different behavior proves one aircraft's automation is broken.

questions.question: Why does a navigation display need to be interpreted with aircraft state and mode information?

expected_key_facts.fact: The display may show a plan, prediction, selected target, or measured result.
Mode and aircraft state determine how the displayed information relates to actual guidance.

acceptable_concepts: A line or symbol on a display is not self-explanatory.
Cross-check the active mode, source, and aircraft response.
important_incorrect_concepts: The drawn route is proof that the aircraft is tracking it.
Display geometry alone identifies the active guidance source.

questions.question: Why should engine indications be compared with thrust mode and aircraft response?

expected_key_facts.fact: An engine parameter can show a measured value while the thrust mode expresses a target or control context.
Aircraft acceleration, speed trend, and configuration provide independent response evidence.

acceptable_concepts: Use the indication, active mode, and aircraft trend as separate evidence.
A single parameter should not be treated as the whole explanation.
important_incorrect_concepts: One engine display value always proves the commanded thrust.
Autothrust means thrust cannot change with condition.

questions.question: Why is source awareness important when explaining an A321neo system?

expected_key_facts.fact: Public conceptual information may not specify an aircraft's exact implementation or procedure.
Aircraft standard, software, engine option, operator, and current approved documentation control operational details.

acceptable_concepts: Separate a general principle from a claim about a particular aircraft or operation.
State uncertainty and identify the authoritative source needed.
important_incorrect_concepts: A general web explanation overrides the operator manual.
One A321neo configuration represents every A321neo.

questions.question: Why is it risky to diagnose a hydraulic or electrical problem from one indication alone?

expected_key_facts.fact: An indication may represent one sensor, state, or subsystem rather than the whole aircraft function.
Independent indications and actual aircraft effects help distinguish data, configuration, and system causes.

acceptable_concepts: Use multiple cues and system relationships.
A symptom should be separated from the cause being inferred.
important_incorrect_concepts: One caution or value identifies the failed component with certainty.
The displayed status cannot be wrong or incomplete.

questions.question: Why do takeoff and landing performance questions require more than aircraft weight?

expected_key_facts.fact: Runway, wind, temperature, pressure altitude, slope, surface, obstacles, configuration, and weight can all matter.
The interaction must be evaluated with approved aircraft-specific data.

acceptable_concepts: Performance is a multi-input calculation, not a weight-only lookup.
The approved result is tied to the aircraft and conditions.
important_incorrect_concepts: Weight alone determines a safe runway distance.
A generic chart is valid for every runway and variant.

questions.question: How does an A320-family flight-control computer turn a pilot input into aircraft response?

expected_key_facts.fact: The computer receives pilot input and aircraft-state information.
Applicable control laws calculate commands for actuators or control surfaces.
The result depends on the active law, configuration, and aircraft condition.

acceptable_concepts: Input, sensing, computation, actuation, and feedback form the chain.
The chain is not a fixed one-to-one mechanical mapping.
important_incorrect_concepts: The computer merely relays a mechanical sidestick movement.
The same input always produces the same surface movement in every law.

questions.question: How does autothrust differ from a pilot directly setting engine thrust?

expected_key_facts.fact: Autothrust is an automatic thrust-management function using targets and mode logic.
Thrust-lever position and engine-control behavior are related but not identical to a simple manual thrust command.
The crew must monitor mode, indications, and aircraft response.

acceptable_concepts: The system manages thrust in a control context while lever position can provide a reference.
Explain target, mode, measured parameter, and response separately.
important_incorrect_concepts: Autothrust directly controls airspeed without regard to aircraft state.
The levers always move continuously to show the exact commanded thrust.

questions.question: How does an ILS provide guidance conceptually?

expected_key_facts.fact: The system provides lateral and vertical deviation information from approach signals.
The aircraft and flight guidance use the received information subject to mode, signal, and configuration conditions.

acceptable_concepts: Localizer-like lateral and glideslope-like vertical information are interpreted as deviations from an approach path.
Signal validity and active mode matter.
important_incorrect_concepts: ILS is a satellite navigation database.
Receiving a signal guarantees an automatic landing in every condition.

questions.question: How does an inertial reference contribute to navigation when satellite input is not the only source?

expected_key_facts.fact: An inertial reference estimates motion and attitude from sensed acceleration and rotation.
Its estimate can support position and guidance computations but accumulates error over time.

acceptable_concepts: Inertial information provides continuity and aircraft-state estimates.
It is one source that can be combined with other navigation inputs.
important_incorrect_concepts: Inertial navigation has no drift.
An inertial reference is the same thing as a navigation database.

questions.question: How does a fuel system support engine operation and aircraft balance?

expected_key_facts.fact: Fuel tanks, pumps, valves, lines, and controls deliver fuel toward the engines.
Fuel quantity and distribution can affect loading, balance, and system status.
Exact transfer logic and limits are aircraft-standard dependent.

acceptable_concepts: Explain delivery, monitoring, and distribution as separate functions.
Fuel management is both propulsion support and mass-distribution management.
important_incorrect_concepts: Fuel is always moved only by gravity.
All A321neo fuel-transfer logic is identical regardless of configuration.

questions.question: How does the pneumatic system support several aircraft functions?

expected_key_facts.fact: A pneumatic network sources, regulates, distributes, and supplies compressed air.
Downstream users can include environmental functions and, depending on configuration, other aircraft services.
Exact sources and availability depend on aircraft standard and operating condition.

acceptable_concepts: Separate source, regulation, distribution, and user functions.
Do not assume every pneumatic source is available in every phase.
important_incorrect_concepts: The pneumatic system is only a passenger-cabin ventilation fan.
All downstream users always receive identical pressure and flow.

questions.question: What should be compared when distinguishing the A321neo from the A321ceo?

expected_key_facts.fact: The labels distinguish new-engine-option and current-engine-option generations.
Engine installation, weight, systems, configuration, and performance can differ.
Exact differences must be verified for the aircraft standard and operator.

acceptable_concepts: Compare propulsion generation plus associated configuration and performance data.
Avoid assuming a single universal neo-versus-ceo difference.
important_incorrect_concepts: CEО means the aircraft has no digital flight controls.
Every A321neo has the same engine and limits as every A321ceo.

questions.question: How are the FCU and MCDU different kinds of flight-deck interface?

expected_key_facts.fact: The FCU is associated with primary flight-guidance selections such as selected targets or modes.
The MCDU is a multipurpose interface for flight-management and related entries or review.
Both require confirmation through indications and aircraft response.

acceptable_concepts: FCU interaction is oriented toward immediate guidance selections; MCDU interaction is broader management and data entry.
They are complementary, not interchangeable.
important_incorrect_concepts: The FCU is the navigation database.
The MCDU directly moves flight-control surfaces.

questions.question: What is the difference between lateral navigation intent and the aircraft's actual ground track?

expected_key_facts.fact: Lateral intent describes a planned or commanded path.
Ground track is the measured direction of movement over the ground.
Wind, aircraft state, guidance mode, and navigation error can create differences.

acceptable_concepts: Compare route or guidance target with actual track and trend.
The aircraft can be pointed one way while moving over the ground another way.
important_incorrect_concepts: Heading and ground track are always identical.
A drawn route proves the actual track is correct.

questions.question: How should a general aircraft principle be compared with a simulator-specific behavior?

expected_key_facts.fact: The general principle explains the intended relationship or mechanism.
Simulator behavior is an implementation that may simplify or configure that relationship.
The simulator cannot by itself establish an approved real-aircraft procedure or limitation.

acceptable_concepts: Use the simulator to explore hypotheses, then verify operational claims elsewhere.
Record model version and assumptions.
important_incorrect_concepts: A simulator output is automatically a certification fact.
A general principle makes every simulated detail universal.

questions.question: What is the useful distinction between a prediction and a measurement on the flight deck?

expected_key_facts.fact: A prediction is computed from assumptions, inputs, and a model.
A measurement or sensed indication describes an observed parameter.
Comparing them can reveal changing conditions, input errors, or model limits.

acceptable_concepts: Treat forecast and observation as separate evidence streams.
A mismatch is a reason to investigate, not proof of a particular fault.
important_incorrect_concepts: Predictions are measurements.
A mismatch automatically identifies a failed sensor.

questions.question: How does energy management differ from simply controlling airspeed?

expected_key_facts.fact: Energy management considers airspeed, altitude, thrust, drag, and flight path together.
Airspeed is one measured part of the aircraft energy state, not the whole state.

acceptable_concepts: A speed target can be met while altitude, path, or thrust state changes.
Use trends and configuration to understand the energy picture.
important_incorrect_concepts: Maintaining airspeed alone guarantees a stable flight path.
Energy management means ignoring airspeed.

questions.question: A selected heading is visible but the aircraft turns differently than expected. What diagnostic sequence is useful?

expected_key_facts.fact: Check what heading or track target was selected and whether the input was accepted.
Check active and armed lateral modes on the FMA.
Compare actual track, wind, aircraft state, and guidance source before concluding a fault.

acceptable_concepts: Separate selection, mode, target type, and measured turn.
Check whether the aircraft is following heading, track, or managed lateral intent.
important_incorrect_concepts: A heading selector always commands an immediate fixed turn.
The difference proves the navigation system failed.

questions.question: A vertical path prediction changes after a mass entry. What should be investigated?

expected_key_facts.fact: Verify the entered mass and related performance inputs.
Check phase, constraints, speed assumptions, and aircraft configuration.
A prediction is computed and must not be mistaken for a guaranteed aircraft trajectory.

acceptable_concepts: Mass changes the model's energy and performance assumptions.
Compare old and new inputs before judging the result.
important_incorrect_concepts: The mass entry cannot affect a vertical prediction.
The prediction alone proves the aircraft will fly that path.
question_requirements: explain why the prediction can change

questions.question: An electrical indication disagrees with the expected system state. How should the observation be framed?

expected_key_facts.fact: Record the indicated source, bus or distribution state, and relevant loads.
Compare the indication with independent system cues and actual affected functions.
Use the applicable aircraft-specific procedure for operational diagnosis.

acceptable_concepts: Describe the symptom without prematurely naming the failed component.
Separate power source, distribution path, indication, and downstream effect.
important_incorrect_concepts: A single bus label identifies the only possible cause.
The indication can be ignored if the load still works.

questions.question: An engine parameter is normal but acceleration is not as expected. What layers should be compared?

expected_key_facts.fact: Compare the selected or commanded thrust context with the engine indication.
Check aircraft weight, configuration, speed, altitude, and environmental conditions.
Use approved procedures and data for a real operational event.

acceptable_concepts: A normal-looking parameter does not prove normal acceleration in every condition.
Use target, measured engine value, and aircraft response as separate layers.
important_incorrect_concepts: One normal parameter rules out every propulsion or performance issue.
Acceleration is independent of weight and configuration.

questions.question: A route contains a discontinuity after editing. What should be checked before continuing the analysis?

expected_key_facts.fact: Review the sequence of legs and the exact edit that created the discontinuity.
Check constraints, transitions, database data, and active leg or guidance.
Do not infer an operationally valid route solely from a simulator or interface display.

acceptable_concepts: Reconstruct route intent and active route separately.
Validate data and procedure applicability.
important_incorrect_concepts: A route without a visible error message is automatically flyable.
Deleting the discontinuity is always the correct action.

questions.question: The aircraft symbol and navigation display disagree with an outside reference. What should be considered?

expected_key_facts.fact: Identify which reference, sensor, display, and navigation source are being compared.
Check data age or quality, alignment or initialization assumptions, and aircraft state.
Avoid declaring a system failure from one disagreement without independent evidence.

acceptable_concepts: Define the two measurements before interpreting the difference.
Use source hierarchy and cross-checks.
important_incorrect_concepts: The outside reference is always correct.
A display mismatch automatically proves the inertial system failed.

questions.question: What is the conceptual role of flight-control laws in an A320-family aircraft?

expected_key_facts.fact: Control laws define how pilot or automatic inputs are transformed into commands.
They use aircraft-state information and can include protections or mode-dependent behavior.

acceptable_concepts: Control laws are the logic layer between intent, sensed state, and actuation.
Their behavior is not a simple fixed surface ratio.
important_incorrect_concepts: Control laws are only mechanical cables.
The same law and protections apply unchanged in every degraded condition.

questions.question: How should the flight director be described without confusing it with the autopilot?

expected_key_facts.fact: The flight director presents guidance commands or cues for the crew.
The autopilot is an automatic flight-control function that can follow guidance.
The two can be related but are not the same function.

acceptable_concepts: FD guidance is displayed to the pilot; AP uses automatic control when engaged.
Both depend on targets, modes, and aircraft state.
important_incorrect_concepts: The flight director physically moves the aircraft.
The autopilot and flight director are always identical.

questions.question: What does a hydraulic system contribute to aircraft control and operation?

expected_key_facts.fact: Hydraulic pressure transmits force to actuators.
Hydraulic power can support flight-control or other aircraft functions depending on system design.
Exact redundancy and availability depend on aircraft standard.

acceptable_concepts: Explain source, pressure, distribution, actuation, and monitoring.
Hydraulics provide power, not the flight-control logic itself.
important_incorrect_concepts: Hydraulic pressure alone decides which surface should move.
Every hydraulic circuit powers every function identically.

questions.question: What is the purpose of electrical distribution rather than just electrical generation?

expected_key_facts.fact: Generation produces electrical power, while distribution routes and manages it.
Buses, protection, switching, and loads determine how functions receive power.
The exact architecture and redundancy are aircraft-specific.

acceptable_concepts: A generator is only one layer of the electrical system.
Distribution and protection affect availability to essential functions.
important_incorrect_concepts: A generator powers every load directly.
Electrical redundancy means every source is interchangeable in every condition.

questions.question: How are cabin pressure and cabin altitude related conceptually?

expected_key_facts.fact: Pressurization manages cabin pressure so cabin altitude remains within intended limits.
Inflow and regulated outflow interact with aircraft altitude and system control.
Exact limits and procedures are aircraft- and operator-specific.

acceptable_concepts: Cabin altitude is a pressure-equivalent concept, not simply the aircraft's geometric altitude.
Control depends on air supply and outflow management.
important_incorrect_concepts: Cabin altitude always equals aircraft altitude.
Opening outflow always increases cabin pressure.

questions.question: What is the conceptual difference between anti-ice and de-ice?

expected_key_facts.fact: Anti-ice seeks to prevent or limit ice accumulation.
De-ice generally refers to removing accumulated ice.
Terminology and exact system operation depend on the aircraft and component.

acceptable_concepts: The concepts differ by timing and purpose: prevention versus removal.
Use the aircraft-specific system description for operational details.
important_incorrect_concepts: Anti-ice guarantees no ice can exist.
Anti-ice and de-ice always describe the same hardware and operation.

questions.question: Why are spoilers useful to discuss as more than speed brakes?

expected_key_facts.fact: Spoiler panels can change lift and drag.
Depending on design and mode, they can contribute to roll control or ground operations.
Their exact scheduling and authority are aircraft-specific.

acceptable_concepts: Discuss aerodynamic effect plus function and mode.
Avoid treating every spoiler panel as only a descent drag device.
important_incorrect_concepts: Spoilers only increase lift.
All spoiler panels always deploy together for the same purpose.

questions.question: What does the landing gear system have to accomplish beyond supporting the aircraft on the ground?

expected_key_facts.fact: The system supports extension, retraction, locking, steering, and braking functions.
Its operation interacts with hydraulic, electrical, flight-control, and weight-on-wheels logic.
Exact indications and procedures must be aircraft-specific.

acceptable_concepts: Landing gear is a coordinated system with mechanical, power, indication, and ground-mode elements.
Ground sensing and braking are distinct from gear support.
important_incorrect_concepts: Landing gear is only a passive set of wheels.
A gear-down indication alone proves every related braking function is normal.

questions.question: Why is a flight-plan discontinuity a reasoning problem rather than merely a display nuisance?

expected_key_facts.fact: A discontinuity can mean the route sequence is not continuously defined for the intended path.
The crew must understand the intended procedure and data before changing the plan.
The active guidance result must be checked after any edit.

acceptable_concepts: Treat it as an unresolved connection between route elements.
Do not apply a memorized edit without knowing the operational intent.
important_incorrect_concepts: Every discontinuity should be deleted automatically.
The display can be ignored if the aircraft is currently stable.

questions.question: How should a pilot distinguish a database procedure from a crew-entered modification?

expected_key_facts.fact: A database procedure is coded source data with defined applicability and structure.
A crew-entered modification changes or supplements the active plan through interface input.
Both require review of constraints, sequencing, and resulting guidance.

acceptable_concepts: Identify the source and status of each leg.
Crew edits do not automatically inherit every property of a published procedure.
important_incorrect_concepts: Any manually entered leg is equivalent to a published procedure.
A database procedure cannot be changed or reviewed.

questions.question: What is the difference between entering a destination and validating an approach concept?

expected_key_facts.fact: Entering a destination supplies an input to the flight-management plan.
An approach concept also involves procedure, runway, transition, constraints, navigation source, and aircraft conditions.
The displayed plan does not by itself authorize or validate an operational approach.

acceptable_concepts: Data entry is only one step; validation includes procedure and aircraft-context checks.
Use current approved sources.
important_incorrect_concepts: Selecting a destination automatically selects a valid approach.
The database entry is an ATC clearance.

questions.question: Why can a computed time or fuel prediction change without a route edit?

expected_key_facts.fact: Predictions depend on inputs such as aircraft state, mass, wind, speed, and configuration.
Changes in assumptions or sensed data can update time and fuel without changing the route geometry.
A prediction remains an estimate rather than a guarantee.

acceptable_concepts: Route and prediction inputs are different dimensions.
Explain the change by tracing input provenance.
important_incorrect_concepts: Only route edits can change the prediction.
The predicted fuel value is a measured tank quantity.

questions.question: How should a source-aware explanation handle a flight-management page whose exact labels vary?

expected_key_facts.fact: Describe the conceptual purpose and data relationship without claiming a universal label or layout.
Exact labels, prompts, and options depend on aircraft standard, software, and operator configuration.
The current approved reference should settle an operational interpretation.

acceptable_concepts: State what is generally true and qualify what is version-dependent.
Ask for the aircraft standard or source if precision is required.
important_incorrect_concepts: One screenshot defines every MCDU version.
A familiar label guarantees identical underlying logic.

questions.question: What should be inferred when a target is visible on the FCU but the FMA shows a different active mode?

expected_key_facts.fact: The FCU value expresses a selected target or input, while the FMA reports active or armed mode status.
Engagement conditions, managed or selected logic, constraints, and aircraft state may explain the difference.

acceptable_concepts: Investigate the relationship rather than assuming the display is contradictory.
Use mode annunciation and aircraft trend to identify what is controlling.
important_incorrect_concepts: The FCU target must always override the FMA.
The FMA can be ignored when a selector value is visible.

questions.question: Why is an armed mode different from an active mode in a flight-deck explanation?

expected_key_facts.fact: An armed mode is prepared to engage when its conditions are met.
An active mode is currently controlling or participating in guidance.
The distinction helps the crew anticipate transitions and monitor behavior.

acceptable_concepts: Use FMA terminology to distinguish readiness from current authority.
A mode can be armed without being the present control mode.
important_incorrect_concepts: Armed and active mean exactly the same thing.
An armed mode is already commanding the aircraft.

questions.question: How should selected versus managed speed be analyzed when the aircraft speed trend changes?

expected_key_facts.fact: Identify whether the speed target is crew-selected or computed or managed.
Check active thrust or pitch-related modes, configuration, and actual trend.
A target does not eliminate the need to monitor achieved speed.

acceptable_concepts: Start with target source, then mode, then measured response.
Explain trend through energy and configuration rather than label alone.
important_incorrect_concepts: Managed speed is always a fixed number.
The selected target guarantees no speed trend.

questions.question: What does mode reversion mean as a concept, and why should explanations avoid inventing a universal trigger?

expected_key_facts.fact: Mode reversion is a change from one guidance or thrust mode to another when logic or conditions require it.
The applicable trigger and annunciation depend on aircraft standard, mode, and situation.
The FMA and approved documentation are needed for an exact interpretation.

acceptable_concepts: Describe the general idea while qualifying exact conditions.
Treat the annunciated result as evidence to interpret.
important_incorrect_concepts: Every mode reversion has the same trigger on all aircraft.
Reversion always means the automation has completely failed.

questions.question: Why should FMA monitoring continue after a crew selection appears to work?

expected_key_facts.fact: The active mode can change as conditions, constraints, or phase change.
The aircraft response may diverge from the initial expectation even when the input was accepted.
Monitoring confirms continuing mode and target behavior.

acceptable_concepts: Selection is an event; monitoring is continuous.
Use FMA, trend, and aircraft state together.
important_incorrect_concepts: Once selected, a mode cannot change.
FMA monitoring is needed only during takeoff.

questions.question: What is the main reasoning difference between takeoff guidance and cruise guidance?

expected_key_facts.fact: Takeoff is a highly configuration- and energy-sensitive phase with immediate runway and obstacle considerations.
Cruise generally emphasizes stable trajectory, navigation, fuel, and system monitoring.
Exact guidance and procedures are aircraft- and operator-specific.

acceptable_concepts: Different phases prioritize different constraints and margins.
Do not transfer a cruise mental model directly to takeoff.
important_incorrect_concepts: Takeoff and cruise use identical priorities.
Cruise requires no mode or system monitoring.

questions.question: How should a climb explanation connect thrust, speed, altitude, and path?

expected_key_facts.fact: Climb performance is an energy-management problem involving thrust, drag, speed, altitude, and aircraft mass.
The selected or managed target and active mode determine how the system seeks the path.
Actual trend must be monitored rather than inferred from target alone.

acceptable_concepts: Explain the trade between speed and climb path without asserting a fixed universal schedule.
Separate command from response.
important_incorrect_concepts: More thrust always means more climb rate regardless of speed and configuration.
A climb target guarantees the aircraft can achieve it.

questions.question: Why is descent planning not equivalent to simply reducing thrust?

expected_key_facts.fact: Descent involves managing path, speed, altitude constraints, drag, configuration, and energy.
Thrust changes are one input among several, not the complete descent strategy.

acceptable_concepts: A descent must satisfy both vertical-path and energy objectives.
Configuration and constraints can change the result.
important_incorrect_concepts: Idle thrust alone guarantees a correct descent path.
Reducing thrust always reduces speed immediately.

questions.question: What should be monitored when transitioning from descent to approach?

expected_key_facts.fact: Monitor active guidance and thrust modes, target changes, speed, path, and configuration.
Confirm the intended approach data and constraints before relying on the resulting guidance.

acceptable_concepts: Treat the transition as a change in energy and mode priorities.
Use independent indications instead of assuming continuity.
important_incorrect_concepts: The descent mode automatically proves approach guidance is configured.
Configuration changes need no monitoring if the path looks stable.

questions.question: Why does landing require both flight-path awareness and configuration awareness?

expected_key_facts.fact: Landing performance and handling depend on speed, path, mass, wind, surface, and configuration.
The crew must compare commanded or displayed targets with actual aircraft response.

acceptable_concepts: A stable path is not the same as a complete landing assessment.
Configuration and environmental conditions affect margins.
important_incorrect_concepts: Landing is safe whenever the aircraft symbol is on the runway centerline.
Configuration has no effect once approach guidance is active.

questions.question: How should cruise monitoring differ from a hands-off assumption?

expected_key_facts.fact: Automation can reduce workload but still requires monitoring of modes, navigation, fuel, weather, and systems.
Changes in inputs or conditions can change predictions and aircraft response.

acceptable_concepts: Cruise monitoring is active supervision, not abandonment of the flight path.
Use trends and independent cues.
important_incorrect_concepts: Automation makes cruise monitoring unnecessary.
A stable moment proves future behavior will remain unchanged.

questions.question: Why can an approach target be correct while the aircraft is still not in the desired energy state?

expected_key_facts.fact: A target is a reference, while actual energy depends on speed, altitude, path, mass, thrust, drag, and configuration.
Trend and aircraft response must be evaluated in addition to the target.

acceptable_concepts: Target validity and achieved state are separate checks.
Explain excess or deficit energy through multiple variables.
important_incorrect_concepts: A correct target guarantees a stable approach.
Energy state can be inferred from speed alone.

questions.question: What makes a takeoff scenario especially sensitive to incorrect assumptions?

expected_key_facts.fact: Takeoff margins depend on aircraft mass, configuration, runway, environment, and obstacles.
Small input or data errors can affect calculated performance and the resulting decision.

acceptable_concepts: Takeoff requires disciplined data provenance and approved calculations.
Avoid replacing a specific calculation with intuition.
important_incorrect_concepts: A familiar runway makes generic performance assumptions safe.
Takeoff margins depend only on engine thrust.

questions.question: How can a phase-of-flight label help organize troubleshooting without proving the cause?

expected_key_facts.fact: The phase gives context for expected configuration, targets, modes, and constraints.
It narrows relevant hypotheses but does not identify the cause by itself.

acceptable_concepts: Use phase as a prior or context, then verify observations.
The same symptom can have different implications in different phases.
important_incorrect_concepts: The phase label proves which system failed.
A symptom has one universal interpretation across all phases.

questions.question: Why should a landing explanation distinguish touchdown, rollout, and ground-operation states?

expected_key_facts.fact: Aircraft state and available functions change as the aircraft transitions from flight to ground operation.
Braking, steering, spoilers, and ground-related logic have distinct roles and conditions.

acceptable_concepts: Do not treat touchdown as one undifferentiated state.
Interpret indications in the current phase and configuration.
important_incorrect_concepts: All flight controls remain in the same mode after touchdown.
Wheel contact alone proves every ground system is available.

questions.question: How does density altitude influence a conceptual explanation of takeoff performance?

expected_key_facts.fact: Higher density altitude generally changes engine, aerodynamic, and acceleration performance.
Temperature, pressure altitude, weight, runway, wind, and configuration must be considered together.
Operational values require approved aircraft-specific data.

acceptable_concepts: Explain density as a combined atmospheric condition, not a single cockpit setting.
Avoid assigning a universal numeric penalty.
important_incorrect_concepts: Density altitude affects only cabin pressurization.
A fixed percentage correction is valid for every aircraft.

questions.question: Why can a tailwind affect takeoff and landing performance differently from a headwind?

expected_key_facts.fact: Wind changes the relationship between airspeed and ground speed.
That changes runway distance and energy considerations for both takeoff and landing.
The applicable result depends on aircraft, runway, and approved calculation.

acceptable_concepts: Reason through relative air and ground motion.
Do not rely on a single intuition about wind without the phase and data context.
important_incorrect_concepts: Wind changes airspeed and ground speed in exactly the same way.
A tailwind has no performance consequence if indicated airspeed is unchanged.

questions.question: What is the reasoning difference between a performance limit and a target?

expected_key_facts.fact: A target is a desired or selected value used for guidance or planning.
A limit is a boundary that must not be exceeded or a condition that constrains operation.
Both require the applicable aircraft-specific source.

acceptable_concepts: Target and limit have different operational meanings.
A target may change while a limit remains a constraint, subject to source.
important_incorrect_concepts: Every target is a hard limit.
Every limit is merely a suggested target.

questions.question: Why does center of gravity belong in a performance discussion even when total mass is known?

expected_key_facts.fact: CG changes moments, trim requirements, stability, and control characteristics.
Those effects can alter performance or margins beyond the total-mass effect.

acceptable_concepts: Total mass and its distribution are separate loading dimensions.
Use the approved envelope and performance method.
important_incorrect_concepts: CG is irrelevant once total mass is known.
Any CG within a generic envelope guarantees identical performance.

questions.question: How should obstacles be included in a takeoff-performance explanation?

expected_key_facts.fact: Obstacles impose a path or climb-performance consideration beyond runway distance alone.
Aircraft mass, configuration, environment, and runway data affect the result.
The approved performance method supplies the applicable result.

acceptable_concepts: Takeoff performance includes both surface-distance and flight-path constraints.
Do not invent a generic obstacle clearance number.
important_incorrect_concepts: Obstacle clearance is unrelated to climb performance.
A runway-length check alone proves takeoff suitability.

questions.question: What does a performance margin mean in a conceptual answer?

expected_key_facts.fact: A margin is the difference between available capability and a required or limiting condition.
It depends on the assumptions, data quality, configuration, and applicable requirement.

acceptable_concepts: A margin is contextual rather than a universal fixed number.
Small or uncertain margins call for source-aware verification.
important_incorrect_concepts: Margin means the aircraft can ignore a limit.
A generic positive margin is valid regardless of conditions.

questions.question: Why should a model answer avoid quoting an unverified A321neo takeoff number?

expected_key_facts.fact: Takeoff numbers depend on aircraft configuration, mass, atmosphere, runway, obstacles, and assumptions.
A credible number must come from current approved aircraft-specific performance data.

acceptable_concepts: Explain the factors and direct the reader to the authoritative calculation.
A conceptual answer can be useful without fabricating a value.
important_incorrect_concepts: One published-looking number applies to every A321neo.
A model may estimate a legal takeoff limit from general knowledge.
question_requirements: explain why the number is unsafe

questions.question: In a simulator, the FMA changes earlier than expected during climb. How should the trainee study it?

expected_key_facts.fact: Record the prior and new FMA states and the selected or managed targets.
Check altitude, speed, configuration, constraints, and software or model assumptions.
Compare the simulator behavior with authoritative conceptual or aircraft-specific references without treating it as proof.

acceptable_concepts: Analyze transition conditions and state, not just the label.
Change one input at a time.
important_incorrect_concepts: Early mode change automatically means a bug.
A simulator's FMA timing is universal across aircraft standards.
question_requirements: separate model behavior from aircraft authority

questions.question: A simulated engine start shows a different indication than a study guide. What should be compared?

expected_key_facts.fact: Compare aircraft or engine variant, simulator version, modeled sequence, and indication definitions.
Separate generic engine-start principles from exact procedural indications.
Use current approved documentation for operational conclusions.

acceptable_concepts: Check whether the guide and model describe the same configuration.
Treat discrepancy as a source and model-comparison problem first.
important_incorrect_concepts: The study guide or simulator must be universally correct.
A different indication proves the engine is unsafe.

questions.question: A simulator shows no predicted fuel change after a route extension. What hypotheses should be tested?

expected_key_facts.fact: Verify that the route edit is active and included in the computed plan.
Check mass, wind, speed, fuel model, data source, and software version.
A simulator result is an observation to explain, not an operational fuel guarantee.

acceptable_concepts: Use a hypothesis table and vary one assumption at a time.
Distinguish stale display, inactive edit, model simplification, and input issue.
important_incorrect_concepts: No displayed change proves no fuel will be used.
The route length is the only fuel-prediction input.

questions.question: A simulated hydraulic failure changes flight-control behavior. How should the result be interpreted?

expected_key_facts.fact: Record the simulated failure, affected indications, active control law or mode, and aircraft response.
Check the simulator's modeled architecture and aircraft standard.
Do not generalize simulated behavior into a real procedure without approved references.

acceptable_concepts: Trace power availability to control-law and response changes.
Treat the result as model-specific until verified.
important_incorrect_concepts: Every hydraulic failure produces the same law change.
The simulator alone establishes the aircraft's certified behavior.

questions.question: During a simulated RNAV approach, the displayed path and aircraft track diverge. What should be separated?

expected_key_facts.fact: Separate programmed path, active guidance mode, navigation position, and measured ground track.
Check database procedure, wind, aircraft state, simulator model, and display scaling or assumptions.
An observed divergence does not by itself identify the cause or validate a real approach.

acceptable_concepts: Use layers of intent, computation, indication, and response.
Reproduce the result after changing one variable.
important_incorrect_concepts: The path line is the measured track.
Any simulator RNAV path is an approved approach procedure.

questions.question: A virtual A321neo and A320neo show the same selected mode but different speed trends. What is a reasonable study plan?

expected_key_facts.fact: Hold mode, target, environment, mass, configuration, and initial state constant where possible.
Compare engine, aerodynamic, model, and aircraft-standard differences.
Do not infer operational interchangeability from one simulated comparison.

acceptable_concepts: Use a controlled comparison and identify confounders.
Same mode label does not mean same dynamics or performance.
important_incorrect_concepts: Same selected mode must yield identical speed trends.
The larger aircraft has no configuration-dependent difference.

questions.question: A simulator trainee changes one input and several displays update. How can causality be studied?

expected_key_facts.fact: Record the initial state, changed input, timing, display changes, and aircraft response.
Repeat the test with one controlled change and compare expected relationships.
A correlated display change is not automatically proof of a causal mechanism.

acceptable_concepts: Use before-and-after observations and repeatability.
Trace signals through source, computation, indication, and response.
important_incorrect_concepts: The first display that changes is necessarily the cause.
One simulator run proves a universal rule.

questions.question: A model omits a system detail found in a technical reference. What is the correct conclusion?

expected_key_facts.fact: The model may intentionally simplify, abstract, or omit details.
The reference describes a different level of fidelity or an aircraft-specific implementation.
The difference should be documented rather than silently treated as a real-aircraft fact.

acceptable_concepts: Identify the model boundary and keep conceptual and operational claims separate.
Check version and scope.
important_incorrect_concepts: The omitted detail does not exist on the real aircraft.
Every technical reference detail must appear in every simulator.

questions.question: In a simulator approach, a crew selection is accepted but no expected capture occurs. What evidence should be logged?

expected_key_facts.fact: Log the selected target, active and armed modes, capture conditions, aircraft state, and trend.
Log navigation or data source, constraints, configuration, and simulator version.
Use the evidence to compare an input issue, condition issue, data issue, or model issue.

acceptable_concepts: Create a reproducible observation record before interpreting.
Do not collapse all causes into 'autopilot failure'.
important_incorrect_concepts: A failed capture proves the real aircraft would fail.
The selected target is sufficient evidence for expected capture.
